lead: Reciprocity swaps the source and the response in a linear bilateral network. Millman's theorem collapses parallel branches into one voltage source plus one resistor, so a node voltage appears in a single line. Tellegen's theorem says the signed sum of v_k i_k over every branch is zero when KCL and KVL hold. These three results are checks and shortcuts: reciprocity validates transfer measurements, Millman solves parallel-source nodes quickly, and Tellegen audits power balance in any circuit, linear or not.
prereq: You need nodal analysis for KCL at a node and the source transformation step used in Thevenin's theorem.

blocks.text: Reciprocity is a property of linear bilateral networks. Bilateral means every element behaves the same in both directions; resistors, inductors and capacitors qualify. Dependent sources normally break it.

Take a network with no dependent sources. Turn off every other independent source: short every voltage source and open every current source, leaving only the single source used for the test. Put an ideal voltage source V_s in branch 1 and measure current I_2 in branch 2. Now remove the source, put the same V_s in branch 2, and measure current I_1 in branch 1. Reciprocity says I_1 = I_2. The ratio I_2/V_s is the same as I_1/V_s. A current-source form also holds under the same condition: with branch 2 open, a current source in branch 1 produces voltage V_2 across branch 2; with branch 1 open and the same source placed in branch 2, it produces the same voltage V_1 across branch 1.

The theorem does not say all currents stay unchanged. Only the swapped source and response pair has the same value. Use it to avoid a second measurement or a second full solution. In lab work, if a reciprocal network gives different transfer readings after swapping source and meter, the network contains a dependent source, an active device, or a wiring error.

Millman's theorem handles parallel branches between two nodes A and B. Each branch is a voltage source V_k in series with R_k. Let B be reference. V_k is positive when its positive terminal faces A. Source transformation turns branch k into a current source V_k/R_k in parallel with R_k. All current sources add and all resistors combine.

blocks.where: V_AB is the node voltage from A to B in volts; V_k is the source voltage in branch k in volts, positive at A; R_k is the branch resistance in ohms; the sums run over all parallel branches.

blocks.text: Branch current from A to B is I_k = (V_AB − V_k)/R_k. Current into A is J_k = (V_k − V_AB)/R_k. Nodes A and B are the only nodes of the parallel group, so the branch currents into A are the only currents at that node; hence Σ J_k = 0. If a further element or source connects to A, its current must be included in the KCL sum at A.

items: Give each source a sign: plus if its positive terminal faces A, minus if it faces B.
Compute numerator Σ V_k/R_k and denominator Σ 1/R_k with the same branch order.
Divide to get V_AB. Substitute back for any branch current.

blocks.text: If a branch has no source, set V_k = 0; it still contributes 1/R_k to the denominator. The formula also works with conductances: V_AB = Σ V_k G_k / Σ G_k.

Tellegen's theorem applies to any network that satisfies KCL and KVL. It does not need linear elements. Number the branches k = 1 to b. Let v_k be the voltage across branch k and i_k the current through it. Use the passive sign convention: i_k enters the positive terminal of v_k. Then

blocks.where: v_k is the voltage across branch k in volts; i_k is the current through branch k in amperes, entering the positive terminal; the sum runs over all b branches and has units of watts.

blocks.text: The sum is over all branches, and each term v_k i_k is the power absorbed by that branch in watts. A resistor has positive v_k i_k. A source that delivers power has negative v_k i_k. The theorem is conservation of power written branch by branch: total absorbed power is zero.

Use Tellegen as an audit. After solving a circuit, compute v_k i_k for every element and add. A nonzero sum means a sign error, a missing branch, or a KCL/KVL slip. Because the statement depends only on KCL and KVL, it is an instantaneous statement: it holds for nonlinear resistors, time-varying elements and dependent sources at every instant, using the v_k and i_k of that instant. Only a few universities ask for the full proof; the statement and the power check are the examinable core.

spec.title: Millman collapse
spec.aria: Three source-resistor branches feed a Millman node, which gives a node voltage of 5.14 volts.

examples.question: Three parallel branches join nodes A and B. Branch 1: 10 V source in series with 2 Ω. Branch 2: 4 V source in series with 1 Ω. Branch 3: 0 V source in series with 4 Ω. All source positives face A. Find V_AB and the three branch currents into A.
steps: Take B as reference, so V_B = 0 V. All source positives face A, so V_1 = 10 V, V_2 = 4 V, V_3 = 0 V.
examples.answer: V_AB = 5.143 V; the currents into A are 2.429 A, −1.143 A and −1.286 A, so the negative signs mean those two currents leave A.

traps: Using Millman's formula with V_k entered as a magnitude only. A source whose positive terminal faces B must enter the numerator as −V_k.
Applying reciprocity with a dependent source present, or with a nonlinear element. The theorem needs a linear bilateral network.
Thinking reciprocity keeps every current unchanged. Only the swapped source-and-response pair has the same value.
In Tellegen's sum, dropping the passive sign convention. If current leaves the positive terminal, v_k i_k is negative.
Confusing Millman's theorem with Thevenin's theorem. Millman gives one node voltage directly; Thevenin replaces a two-terminal network seen from a load.

quiz.q: State Tellegen's theorem and the sign convention.
quiz.a: For any network satisfying KCL and KVL, Σ v_k i_k = 0 over all branches, with i_k entering the positive terminal of v_k; each term is absorbed power in watts.

quiz.q: Why does a dependent source usually stop reciprocity from applying?
quiz.a: A dependent source makes branch relations directional: its value depends on another branch, so swapping source and response changes the controlling variable and the transfer ratio. Reciprocity needs linear bilateral elements only.

quiz.q: Two branches join A and B. Branch 1: 12 V source, positive at A, in series with 3 Ω. Branch 2: 6 V source, positive at A, in series with 6 Ω. Find V_AB by Millman's theorem.
A 10 V source drives a 2 Ω resistor. Current is 5 A leaving the source's positive terminal. Apply Tellegen's theorem with the passive sign convention.
quiz.a: Resistor: v = 10 V, i = 5 A, p = 50 W. Source: v = 10 V, current entering positive terminal is −5 A, p = −50 W. Sum = 50 − 50 = 0 W.

quiz.q: A 5 V source in branch 1 gives 2 mA in branch 2 of a linear bilateral network. What current does the same 5 V source in branch 2 give in branch 1?
Three parallel branches: 10 V/2 Ω, 4 V/1 Ω, 0 V/4 Ω, all positives at A. Find the current into A from branch 2.

beyond: Not for the exam. Tellegen's theorem is used in power-system loss allocation and in model-order reduction, where an energy balance must survive approximation. Millman's formula appears in sensor arrays and current-summing nodes with many parallel sources. Reciprocity is the basis of reciprocal two-port and antenna measurements, including S12 = S21 in a reciprocal microwave network. Search "Tellegen theorem power balance", "Millman theorem sensor", and "reciprocity S-parameters".
